title: Three companions
hook: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala are killed in Delhi for refusing to give up their faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pandits of Kashmir, led by Kirpa Ram, who traveled to Anandpur for help. Your line was they came to him.

This is a hard day in the story, so it goes gently. After listening to the pandits, Guru Tegh Bahadur decided to go to Delhi himself, to stand for them before the emperor. He did not go alone. A few close companions went with him, men who had served him for years. Tradition says they were arrested on the way and brought to Delhi in chains. The authorities wanted the Guru to give up his faith, and he would not. So, tradition says, they tried to break him by making him watch what happened to his friends. Today, three names Sikhs say with love.
screen: `A HARD DAY, WALKED GENTLY.` → `ARRESTED ON THE ROAD.` → `THREE FRIENDS OF THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Their names were Bhai Mati Das, his younger brother Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayala. Bhai means brother, the title Sikhs give to respected members of the community. Mati Das and Sati Das were brothers from a Brahmin family who served as the Guru's close aides and scribes. Dayala was a devoted companion from the same circle. In Delhi, in November 1675, each of them was offered the same bargain: give up your faith and live. Each refused. And each was put to death, tradition says in front of the Guru, in the old city, near where Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands today. Tradition remembers the manner of each death in painful detail, and Sikhs recall it every year. Here, only this much: they were killed with great cruelty, and they did not bend. What Sikhs hold onto is how they faced it. Tradition says Bhai Mati Das was reciting the Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, which you met near the start of this path, and kept reciting to the end. Tradition says each of the three stayed calm, and kept the Name. None of them was a Guru. They were ordinary members of the community, a scribe, his brother, a friend, and they are remembered today in the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say together, among those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. The Sikh story honors not only its Gurus, but the companions who stood beside them.
screen: `MATI DAS, SATI DAS, DAYALA.` · `DELHI, NOVEMBER 1675.` · `RECITING TO THE END.` · `REMEMBERED IN THE ARDAS.` · then, large: `THEY DID NOT BEND.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, light it; if not, just picture one, and watch the flame. Let the three names move slowly through your mind, Mati Das, Sati Das, Dayala, then widen your thoughts to anyone, anywhere, who has suffered for holding to what they believe. You don't need words; just keep the flame company, and breathe.
Three companions. Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, the Guru's friends, killed in Delhi in 1675 for refusing to give up their faith.
Your line: they did not bend. A scribe, his brother and a friend, remembered in prayer to this day. Seventy-eight days now.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala among the martyrs recalled in the Ardas, and a museum and memorials near Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi honor them.

chat.says: Who were the three companions killed in Delhi before Guru Tegh Bahadur?
options: Mati Das, Sati Das and Dayala: ordinary Sikhs who would not give up their faith.
Three of the Guru's own sons, each of them in line to lead after him.
Three guards who refused the order to harm the Guru, and paid for it.

notes: The manner of each death (sawn, burned in cotton, boiled) is deliberately not described; confirm Keepers are comfortable with this restraint.
Mati Das and Sati Das described as brothers from a Brahmin (Mohyal) family, aides and scribes; Bhai Dayala's background kept general. Confirm.
Arrest location (tradition varies: Ropar, Agra, Malikpur Rangharan) left unnamed. Confirm.

The Ardas does not name them individually in every version; it remembers those who were sawn, burned, boiled. Confirm the phrasing 'their names are spoken today in the Ardas' or soften to 'remembered in the Ardas'.
